name: Survivorship Bias
description: When you only look at the cases that made it through the funnel, you can draw the wrong lesson about what causes success or failure. Visible winners are not a representative sample.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to product analytics, case-study-driven design advice, startup benchmark copying, retained-user interviews, and funnel analyses that ignore who dropped out or never appeared in the data.
prevalence_note: Frequently invoked in analytics, experimentation, and startup case-study critique, but not usually taught as a core mainstream interaction-design law.

findings.description: A statistical reexamination of Abraham Wald's actual WWII aircraft-vulnerability work found his real method was more sophisticated than the popular retelling suggests: Wald didn't simply argue 'reinforce where the returning planes have no bullet holes' — he built a formal statistical model estimating the true, unobserved damage distribution across all planes, including the ones that never made it back, from the damage patterns visible only on survivors, explicitly correcting for the selection bias built into the available data. The popular design/business retelling of 'survivorship bias' as a simple rule of thumb flattens a genuinely rigorous piece of applied statistics.
findings.source_title: Abraham Wald's Work on Aircraft Survivability
findings.source_venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association

findings.description: Using a mutual fund dataset explicitly constructed to be free of survivor bias (including defunct funds), found that apparent performance persistence is almost completely explained by common risk factors and investment expenses rather than manager skill -- a quantitative demonstration of how excluding non-surviving cases (the standard survivorship-bias failure mode) would have produced a misleading appearance of skill-driven predictability. Independently quantifies the survivorship-bias mechanism in a concrete financial-analytics domain, distinct from src-mangel-1984's historical aircraft-armor reexamination -- closes this topic's single-study-risk gap with a different domain and a precise, replicated methodology (survivor-bias-free sampling) rather than a conceptual correction alone.
findings.source_title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance

applications.title: Two NFL comeback stories, same page, same superstition -- survivorship bias in sports journalism
applications.description: Freakonomics highlights a real example from the September 2009 USA Today sports section: on the same page, two separate articles covered fourth-quarter comebacks by heavily-favored NFL teams on Monday Night Football -- the Patriots' comeback win over the Bills and the Chargers' comeback win over the Raiders -- each crediting the comeback to a specific pep-talk moment from a star player (Tom Brady quoted by Randy Moss; LaDainian Tomlinson quoted by teammates). The piece points out that this pattern of attributing wins to a locker-room rallying quote is a form of survivorship bias: such quotes are surely said just as often before losses, but only get reported and remembered when the team happens to win.
applications.ethical_note: An observation about a common, largely harmless journalistic narrative habit (crediting wins to locker-room quotes) rather than any deliberate manipulation of an audience.
